• Common names: Elegance coral, Elegant coral, Wonder coral, Ridge coral
  • Minimum tank size: 60 litres
  • Keeping: Moderate; propagation: Difficult
  • Lighting: Moderate; water flow: Moderate to high
  • Temperature: 23–28°C; salinity SG 1.023–1.025; pH 8.1–8.4; KH 8–12; nitrate less than 20 ppm
  • Feeding: Photosynthetic; tank placement: Bottom; growth rate: Slow
  • Toxicity: Yes; temper: Aggressive
  • Colour: fluorescent green, typically with cream, brown, lime green, red, blue, purple, pink or orange-tipped tentacles

Size, colour and place of collection affect the price. Ask the seller about the origin: specimens from Australia are usually free of ECS, which cannot be said of Indonesian specimens. Indonesian corals have better and more colour variations, but a much lower survivability, while Australian ones are reported to be hardier. Indonesian specimens have been under restriction in recent years but are still sold.

Observe the polyps carefully before taking the coral home to make sure it did not sustain severe injuries during collection or shipping. Avoid specimens with retracted polyps, slimy mucus and pale colouration. Do not buy anything from a store where you see bubble algae, glass anemones (Aiptasia), Asterina starfish or vermetid snails.

Catalaphyllia is a monotypic genus of stony coral in the family Euphylliidae, closely related to Euphyllia (hammer coral, frogspawn, torch corals, etc.). It was first named Pectinia jardinei by William Saville-Kent in 1893, was later referred to as Catalaphyllia plicata (Wells, 1971), and is now known as Catalaphyllia jardinei.

The Elegance coral can be found on reefs throughout the Pacific Ocean, though it is rare in the West Indo-Pacific. Its range also extends to Indonesia, Japan, Australia, Micronesia, Mozambique and Vanuatu.

This coral occurs at depths down to 40 m, in shallow and midwater parts of a reef, preferably in turbid waters. It is mostly collected from deep flats with sandy bottoms, lagoons, seagrass beds and near-shore mudflats.
The minimum tank size is 60 litres. A larger tank is even better, as it allows adequate spacing between corals and gives more stable water chemistry.

In specimens not suffering from Elegance Coral Syndrome (ECS) the care level is rated Moderate, while infected corals stand no chance of surviving, as the disease has no known cure. The coral is therefore not ideal for beginner reef keepers.

Place it on the bottom of the tank, on the sand bed rather than live rock, which can injure its delicate polyps. Before removing an expanded colony from the water, make the polyps retract temporarily by fanning them underwater, as expanded polyps are easily damaged.

It needs moderate lighting, moderate water flow and regular feeding of shredded meaty foods. Carry out routine partial water changes of 20% a month, 10% every two weeks or 5% weekly.

Problems

Elegance Coral Syndrome (ECS): a lethal infection known to occur only in Catalaphyllia, affecting many specimens in the trade, especially those from Indonesia. Symptoms include swelling of the oral disc and unexpanded polyps, a white opaque mucus-like coating, tentacles unable to capture prey easily and reduced feeding response. The cause and cure are unknown, and it can spread from one Catalaphyllia to another within a short time. Quarantine new Catalaphyllia for a month; if no symptoms appear, move the coral to the display tank. Fragging infected corals is stressful and can kill them.

Brown jelly: a mass of brown jelly or goo caused by poor water quality or tissue damage. Place the coral in a separate container, brush off the jelly, apply broad-spectrum antibiotics to affected areas and keep it in a quarantine tank until it fully recovers.

Coral bleaching: caused by direct lighting, extreme temperatures, changes in salinity, pH, etc. The coral turns pale or translucent as the symbiotic algae are expelled. Find the cause and fix it.

Gall crabs: fairly harmless hitchhikers, but hardy, and they can survive dips during acclimation. They can be removed manually by squeezing them out of the hole with a pin or similar.

Abandoning the base (bailing out): sometimes the coral leaves its old skeleton. The reasons are unknown; the reef community assumes too strong a current and insufficient nutrition. The part that comes loose will usually die, though in rare cases the coral survives and builds a new skeleton. Sometimes it only recedes from the skeleton around the edges, which can happen once every few months. As long as the tissue is not receding, it should bounce back.

• Temperature: 23–28°C
  • pH: 8.1–8.4; constant pH fluctuations can affect the coral's health
  • Hardness: 8–12 dKH
  • Salinity: 1.023–1.025
  • Phosphates: 0–0.05 ppm
  • Ammonia: 0 ppm
  • Nitrate: 5–10 ppm
  • Calcium: 380–450 ppm
  • Magnesium: 1200–1350 ppm
  • Strontium: 8–10 ppm

Elegance corals prefer slightly dirtier water and need a little nitrate and phosphate. As long as no exposed skeleton is visible, the coral is doing well.

Lighting: provide moderate, diffused lighting with PAR values between 50 and 150. The coral needs enough light for its symbiotic zooxanthellae to photosynthesise, but it dislikes intense, direct light, so a strong light may need to be shaded. LED and fluorescent lighting both work; light from metal halides should be diffused to prevent damage to the fleshy polyps. Under actinic lighting the coral glows bright green, the white striations on the oral disc become bolder and the tentacle tips glow in their original colours.

Water flow: moderate flow is generally appreciated. Its natural habitat is turbid water, and stronger flow brings more food to the tentacles, but many aquarists report that currents that are too strong or turbulent tore the polyps or made them retract fully.

Substrate: Elegance corals do better on a sand bed, which is safer and replicates their natural environment. Rock may scratch their delicate tissue, and damaged tissue can lead to bacterial infection.

The Elegance coral gets a great deal of its nutrition from photosynthesis, through a symbiotic relationship with marine algae (zooxanthellae) living in its tissue. It can also filter-feed, capturing planktonic organisms, small prey and food particles from the water column with its tentacles.

It also benefits from direct or supplemental feeding of small meaty foods, and will accept:

  • mysis shrimp
  • krill
  • brine shrimp (and other similar-sized foods)
  • vitamin-enriched brine shrimp
  • daphnia
  • copepods
  • Reef Roids

Small fish or scallops can also be offered, but must be finely chopped or minced for easy digestion and to prevent regurgitation; do the same for shrimp and krill. Frozen foods should be thawed and rinsed, and chopped food rinsed several more times to remove as much phosphate as possible.

Although some reef keepers have never fed their Elegance corals, feeding 1–2 times a week is recommended, adequately and at the right time, to keep the coral healthy and strong.

This stony coral prefers to be mounted on soft substrate at the bottom of the reef tank, where it can easily bury itself. Its stinging tentacles capture small prey and defend it against predators. Like anemones, it has sticky tentacle tips, which help catch and hold prey. Unlike many corals, it has no long sweeper tentacles.

The Elegance coral is highly aggressive to intruding fish and corals, especially those seen as competitors. Keep a spacing of at least 15 cm around it, or neighbouring corals will be severely harmed. Keep it away from corals with stinging tentacles, including its relatives in Euphylliidae such as Euphyllia (anchor, hammer, frogspawn), which can damage it and which it can also harm.

It is aggressive to animals as well. Keeping snails with it is not recommended: it kills snails (Astrea, Nassarius, Mexican Turbo, Cerith, etc.). Peppermint shrimp, skunk cleaner shrimp, blood shrimp, blue leg hermit crabs, Halloween hermit crabs and sea hares have also been caught when they got too close, and there are reports of it capturing 15 cm bristleworms.

Housing it with clownfish (Amphiprion percula) is hit and miss. Without anemones it can often host clownfish without issues, but rarely the clownfish irritate it enough that it retracts its polyps. Try it and see how the coral responds.

In nature, Elegance corals reproduce sexually and asexually.

Sexual reproduction: the coral releases gametes (eggs and sperm), producing a fertilised egg that becomes a free-swimming planula larva. The larva changes into a tiny polyp that begins to exude calcium carbonate to form an exoskeleton. This is very common in the wild, but there is no known case in captivity.

Asexual reproduction: mature corals form daughter colonies, which can be carefully removed from the parent with a sharp razor blade or scissors once their skeletons reach a decent size. A healthy coral produces new buds every few months.

Fragging: possible with an electric wet tile saw, but complicated and risky, with a low survival rate. The tissue is deeply embedded in the skeleton, so hammers, chisels, cutters and other less accurate tools severely damage it. Keep your hands clean or wear gloves. Use a healthy coral of decent size with several mouths and cut so that at least one mouth remains on each piece. Divide the coral with an electric bandsaw, then give an iodine dip.

The Elegance coral is a colonial coral, free-living (rare) or attached, with corallites fused in winding rows joined at the base. Like Euphyllia, colonies are flabello-meandroid, but with straight-edged septa forming V-shaped valleys not found in Euphyllia. Free-living forms are smaller, on soft substrates, with a V-shaped skeletal base. The polyps have long flowing tubular tentacles with contrasting tips extending from large, fleshy striped oral discs.

It can grow up to 30 cm in length and 20 cm in diameter, with tentacles about 10 cm long when fully extended. The polyp itself can be 4 to 5 times larger than the skeleton base. It is very slow-growing.

It was once recommended as an ideal beginner species because of its hardiness, but this changed after the spread of Elegance Coral Syndrome.
